intro.text: Apps work much like websites underneath. Every time you open an app or tap something in it, the app sends a request to its own servers, and each request goes to a specific web address. Two layers of that traffic tell us what is happening.

intro.text: Amazon Prime Video Channels: what viewership and subscriber data a channel partner actually receives

runs.text: Amazon Prime Video Channels: what viewership and subscriber data a channel partner actually receives

paragraphs.text: Amazon publishes the reporting spec for Prime Video Channels, and it is more granular than most people assume. Every channel partner, anywhere in the world, gets episode-level viewing (streams, unique streamers, minutes) plus aggregate subscription, conversion and retention numbers. Larger partners negotiate deeper tiers, down to a daily, one-row-per-stream feed keyed to a stable pseudonymous customer ID. What no partner ever receives is the customer's identity, because Amazon remains the merchant of record. The real question for any Channels partner is not "do you get viewership" but "which tier did you negotiate."

subs.title: The two base-tier reports that matter most, explained

paragraphs.text: Content Usage (weekly and monthly). For every episode, and separately for every subscription plan, four numbers: Total Customers Streamed (unique people who played it), Total Number of Streams (play sessions: a valid stream is anything over 0 seconds through the Prime interface, and pressing play again or switching device starts a new one), Total Minutes Streamed (non-ad minutes) and Total Ad Minutes Streamed. So "how many people, how many times, how many minutes" per episode. There is no completion rate; minutes divided by customers against runtime is the proxy. Because the stream threshold is 0 seconds, stream counts run well above any viewer definition Crosswalk uses.

paragraphs.text: • Amazon reports only to its contracting partner. The Channels reports go to the channel operator (Peacock). WBD is not a party to the Peacock and Amazon agreement and receives nothing from Amazon for that lane. Amazon's Terms of Use say it shares non-identifiable viewing history with "video content providers offering subscription services through Prime Video add-on subscriptions," meaning the channel, not the channel's licensors.• Peacock itself sees the Channels lane only through Amazon's reports. Playback happens inside the Prime Video app and player, so Peacock has no first-party telemetry on those sessions. For most partners that means aggregate episode-level usage; only a Tier 1 partner gets session rows.• What WBD gets depends on the WBD and Peacock license, not on Amazon. Licensors typically receive aggregate title-level performance (hours or views per title, often quarterly) for the service in total. A lane split (Peacock app vs Amazon vs other storefronts) is unusual and exists only if negotiated. Amazon's General Terms bind the partner to use information obtained under the agreement only for that agreement's purposes, so Peacock would normally pass its own derived aggregates, not Amazon's reports.• Not all platforms, and not the whole lane. There is no industry standard. Netflix publishes semiannual hours viewed per title but gives licensors little beyond it. The 2023 WGA and SAG-AFTRA agreements force the major services (Peacock, Max, Prime Video, Netflix and others) to report quarterly hours viewed for high-budget programs, but to the guilds under confidentiality, not to licensors. Performance-based license deals now specify metrics, cadence, format and audit rights; that is where a licensor gets lane detail, if at all.• Crosswalk implication. A licensor sees its title on a platform as one aggregate number, if that, and cannot see who watched, through which storefront, or what else they watch. Crosswalk observes the viewer at the device level regardless of who billed them. Peacock app vs Prime Video is a deterministic split (different hosts and URLs). Inside Prime Video, the play URL names the title but not the entitlement, so the Peacock lane is assigned by catalog rights (the title is on Prime Video only through the Peacock add-on in the window) or by the household's channel sign-up and manage-channel signals. Titles reachable by two routes at once without an entitlement signal stay attributed to Prime Video, not to Peacock.
